India Over 1,700 swine flu cases logged in Delhi this year amid surge in seasonal influenza infections PTI 21 August, 2026 03:49 pm IST Facebook Twitter WhatsApp Linkedin Follow Us : Text Size: A- A+ New Delhi, Aug 21 (PTI) Delhi has registered more than 1,700 cases of swine flu this year, health department officials said on Friday, as the national capital sees a surge in seasonal influenza cases during monsoon. On the day, Delhi Health Minister Pankaj Kumar Singh and representatives of the health department are scheduled to meet Union Health Minister J P Nadda and senior officials from the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to review the swine flu situation in the capital. “A report is being prepared to assess the number of cases and the overall situation. Everything is under control. There is no need for general panic. All government hospitals have been directed to ensure adequate treatment facilities,” Singh told PTI. Show Full Article The minister said the government is closely monitoring the situation and has directed all government hospitals to ensure adequate treatment facilities are available. Healthcare institutions and concerned officials have been told to keep a close watch on infection patterns, affected areas and potential hotspots, the minister said, adding that separate wards are being set up for swine flu patients. Doctors in Delhi said they are seeing a noticeable surge in number of patients with influenza and influenza-like symptoms, though most cases are mild to moderate. Dr Rishikesh Desai, consultant physician in the department of internal medicine at Sir Ganga Ram Hospital, said the hospital is witnessing a rise in seasonal influenza cases. “Most healthy individuals recover well, but influenza can become serious in older adults, pregnant women, young children and people with chronic diseases,” he said. Dr Neha Rastogi Panda, senior consultant in the department of infectious diseases at Fortis Hospital, Gurugram, also recounted a similar situation. “There has been a sudden increase in patients with influenza and influenza-like illnesses,” she said. “Most patients have mild to moderate illness and recover well with appropriate supportive care, so there is no reason to panic.” Rastogi further said doctors were seeing more prolonged cough and greater intensity of fever this season, possibly due to reactive inflammation of the lungs due to air pollution, particularly from particulate pollutants. According to medical practitioners, H1N1 infection — commonly known as swine flu — usually presents fever, cough, sore throat, headache, body aches and fatigue. Those with persistent high fever, breathing difficulty, chest pain, confusion or worsening symptoms are advised to seek medical attention promptly. “Vaccination, hand hygiene, avoiding close contact while ill and staying home during the infection period are key to limiting transmission,” Dr Desai said. Khader chairing a review meeting in Bengaluru on Monday (August 24) with senior health officials from the State and districts to assess the H1N1 spread situation and preparedness. | Photo Credit: Special Arrangement The Karnataka Health Department has stepped up surveillance and preparedness measures for seasonal influenza, including H1N1, with the State recording 4,212 laboratory-confirmed cases this year across 32 districts till August 22. The department said the rise in cases being reported during the monsoon was part of the usual seasonal pattern and urged people not to panic. In Karnataka, influenza generally records two seasonal peaks — from January to March and July to September. Health Minister U.T. Khader chaired a review meeting on Monday (August 24) with senior health officials to assess the situation and preparedness. The State’s health system has adequate infrastructure and essential medicines to handle the situation, he said. According to surveillance data on the Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP), Karnataka has reported 4,212 laboratory-confirmed influenza-positive cases till August 22. This compares with 4,583 cases reported in 2025 and 3,903 cases in 2024. Over 50% of the 4,212 cases reported this year are from GBA limits. Addressing presspersons after the meeting, the Minister said it was closely monitoring the situation through strengthened surveillance of influenza-like illness (ILI) and severe acute respiratory infections (SARI). Surveillance strengthened The State has designated sentinel surveillance sites under the ICMR-NCDC network for monitoring respiratory viruses. The Viral Research and Diagnostic Laboratories (VRDL) network is also being used to ensure timely collection and testing of samples. Adequate laboratory consumables were being made available to support testing and early detection, he said. Health facilities across the State have been instructed to maintain adequate stocks of essential supplies, including personal protective equipment, N95 masks and oseltamivir. Healthcare workers have been sensitised on the early identification of ILI and SARI cases, assessment of risk and appropriate management. Private hospitals and healthcare facilities have also been advised to follow the State’s protocols for screening, testing and treatment of H1N1 cases. They have been asked to mandatorily report cases to the surveillance authorities through the IHIP platform. The Minister said the department has strengthened infection prevention and control measures in healthcare facilities and is focusing on respiratory hygiene, cough etiquette and hand hygiene. Public awareness campaigns are also being intensified. ‘Take precautions’ The department has advised people with symptoms to visit the nearest government health facility. People have been asked to cover their nose and mouth while coughing or sneezing, wash their hands regularly with soap and water, drink plenty of fluids and isolate themselves when symptomatic. They have also been advised to avoid touching their eyes, nose and mouth, refrain from self-medication and avoid shaking hands or visiting crowded places when they have symptoms. Reusing napkins has also been discouraged. The Minister said seasonal influenza could be prevented and managed through early detection and timely treatment, particularly among high-risk groups. He said the reports had caused concern among parents, with some keeping their children away from school. On the day, Singh attended a meeting chaired by Union Health Minister J P Nadda to review Delhi’s preparedness to treat seasonal influenza and vector-borne diseases. In an official statement issued after the meeting, Singh said there was no shortage of beds, doctors, medicines or essential medical equipment in the capital, adding that the patient tally was being monitored, and hospital arrangements being strengthened according to requirements. Show Full Article According to the statement, the Delhi State Health Mission is maintaining close surveillance through the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP), with daily monitoring of influenza-like illness (ILI), severe acute respiratory infection (SARI) and influenza cases reported through the IDSP-IHIP (Integrated Health Information Platform) portal. Regular updates are being shared with senior authorities. Advisories have been issued to chief district medical officers, district surveillance officers and hospitals for screening, reporting and monitoring of ILI, SARI and influenza cases, the statement said, adding that technical guidelines covering patient categorisation, treatment protocols, ventilatory management, masks and home care have also been circulated. Healthcare workers are being sensitised and trained on symptoms and follow-up protocols, while a refresher training programme for district officers was held recently, the statement said. An inter-sectoral meeting involving the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD), New Delhi Municipal Council (NDMC), Delhi Cantonment Board, education department, Delhi Development Authority (DDA) and other stakeholders has directed that public awareness and IEC (information, education, and communication) activities on influenza prevention and control be intensified, it said. Of the total influenza-A cases, 1,777 were reported to be H1N1 infections, commonly known as swine flu, while 37 were H1, 138 were H3 and 440 were categorised as other influenza cases, according to the Delhi government. H1N1 is the predominant strain in the city. Additionally, Delhi has reported 246 dengue cases and 80 malaria cases this year, with zero deaths from either disease. Chikungunya cases stood at 19, also with no deaths. As part of vector-control measures, local bodies have conducted 2.38 crore house visits, sprayed 3.20 lakh houses, identified 91,217 mosquito-positive houses, issued 74,591 legal notices and launched 6,724 prosecutions, the statement said. Delhi has 35 designated sentinel surveillance hospitals, two apex referral laboratories at AIIMS and NCDC, and a malaria reference laboratory at Maulana Azad Medical College. Hospitals have been directed to maintain mosquito-free campuses, ensure timely reporting and keep adequate diagnostic kits, medicines, intravenous fluids, blood products and dedicated beds wherever required, the statement said. The Delhi government is coordinating with the MCD, NDMC, Delhi Cantonment Board and other departments for prevention and control, while dengue and malaria surveillance, training, awareness and door-to-door outreach through ASHA workers continue, it added. According to the statement, Delhi’s malaria annual parasite incidence remains below one, placing it in the pre-elimination phase, with the “Test, Track and Treat” strategy being implemented under the 2025-27 malaria elimination plan. The complete preparedness report of Delhi has been shared with Union Health Minister J P Nadda, including arrangements for beds, doctors, medicines and other essential facilities, Singh said, adding that the Union minister has assured that the Centre will provide every necessary support. Singh urged citizens to follow respiratory hygiene, use masks in crowded places, maintain hand hygiene, avoid close contact with people suffering from respiratory illnesses and consult doctors rather than self-medicate. “Public health preparedness is a continuous process. Our priority is early detection, timely treatment and ensuring adequate hospital capacity,” he added. PTI SGV ARB ARB This report is auto-generated from PTI news service. records.content: News Business Arts & Culture Our Magazine Sports ET Scenes Haya Karima News Business Arts & Culture ET Scenes Our magazine Sports VACSERA to supply over 300,000 doses of seasonal Flu vaccine, says Health Ministry BY Egypt Today staff - Fri, 21 Aug 2026 - 02:25 GMT BY Egypt Today staff Fri, 21 Aug 2026 - 02:25 GMT CAIRO – 21 August 2026: The Ministry of Health and Population announced that the seasonal influenza vaccine will soon be available through the Holding Company for Biological Products and Vaccines (VACSERA), ahead of the winter season and the start of the school year. This initiative aims to safeguard public health and curb the spread of seasonal respiratory viruses. The Ministry highlighted that influenza remains among the most common respiratory illnesses, particularly in schools and crowded settings, underscoring the vital role of vaccination in preventing infection and reducing severe complications. To meet public demand, the Ministry affirmed its commitment to providing a variety of vaccines approved by the Egyptian Drug Authority—including trivalent and quadrivalent formulations—through VACSERA. The inventory exceeds 300,000 doses sourced from global suppliers, including French manufacturer Sanofi, American firm Abbott, and leading South Korean producers. VACSERA will begin rolling out the vaccines on September 1. They will be distributed across 28 centers affiliated with the Serum and Vaccine Institute across various governorates to ensure nationwide coverage. The Ministry noted that the vaccines offer effective immunity for over six months, providing robust protection throughout the flu season. Health authorities strongly encourage all citizens—especially children, the elderly, and individuals with chronic medical conditions—to get vaccinated at authorized centers to protect their families and strengthen community-wide immunity. Isha Deep August 24, 2026 Supported by Delhi has recorded 1,777 H1N1 cases up to August 20, 2026, amid a wider rise in seasonal influenza, but the ICMR has clarified that no new H1N1 strain has been detected in India. The circulating Influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses are similar to the A/Missouri/11/2025 strain, have been circulating since 2025 and are well matched with vaccine strains recommended for the Northern Hemisphere. The rise has nevertheless prompted closer monitoring. Union Health Minister JP Nadda reviewed the situation with Delhi Health Minister Pankaj Kumar Singh and senior officials, focusing on surveillance, testing, early detection and hospital preparedness. Delhi authorities have said hospitals have adequate beds, doctors, medicines and essential equipment. ICMR has stressed that seasonal influenza, including H1N1, is mostly self-limiting, but young children, older people and those with underlying medical conditions can face a higher risk of complications. The current message from health authorities is therefore one of caution without panic: the virus is not new, but a rise in infections still requires responsible monitoring and timely care. Delhi Sees A Sharp Rise In H1N1 Cases According to Delhi government data, 2,392 Influenza A cases had been recorded cumulatively by August 20, of which 1,777 were H1N1 infections. Another 210 cases were attributed to Influenza B, taking the combined Influenza A and B tally to 2,602. H1N1 has consequently emerged as the predominant Influenza A subtype in Delhi this year. The increase is particularly notable when compared with the 229 H1N1 cases recorded during the corresponding period last year. On August 20 alone, 114 new H1N1 cases were reported. The rise has been seen amid seasonal changes and an increase in people presenting with flu-like symptoms. Doctors have said most patients experience familiar influenza symptoms, including fever, cough, sore throat, headache and body aches. Dr Randeep Guleria has noted that H1N1 cases commonly increase during the monsoon, although the current numbers are relatively higher. Older people, young children and those with co-morbidities can be more vulnerable to complications, including breathing difficulties and viral pneumonia. The increase has also triggered a closer look at healthcare preparedness. On August 21, Nadda reviewed the situation and called for continued vigilance, robust surveillance and early identification of unusual increases or clusters. The review covered influenza-like illness and severe acute respiratory infection trends, testing and laboratory surveillance, as well as preparedness across healthcare facilities. ICMR Says No New H1N1 Strain Has Been Detected The rise in cases has naturally raised a key question: does the increase indicate that a new or more dangerous H1N1 virus is circulating? ICMR says no. Senior ICMR scientists have said the Influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses currently circulating in India belong to the A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1)pdm09-like strain. The viruses belong to clade 6B.1A.5a2a and subclade D.3.1.1, and have been circulating since 2025. In other words, the current rise does not indicate the emergence of a newly detected H1N1 strain. ICMR has also said the circulating influenza strains are well matched with vaccine strains recommended for the Northern Hemisphere. It has described seasonal influenza as mostly self-limiting, with most people recovering with appropriate care and rest. At the same time, reassurance does not mean the illness should be dismissed. Health authorities have specifically highlighted young children, older adults and people with underlying medical conditions as groups that can be more vulnerable to complications. Who Is At Risk H1N1 is a contagious respiratory infection. Influenza viruses primarily spread through respiratory droplets and particles released when an infected person coughs or sneezes. People can also become infected after touching contaminated surfaces and then touching their mouth or nose. An infected person may be able to spread influenza from about a day before symptoms appear and for several days afterwards. People who may face a greater risk of complications include: Young children, particularly those with underlying medical conditions. Older adults, who can be more vulnerable to severe influenza. People with underlying or chronic medical conditions, especially when these conditions affect the respiratory system or immune response. People with weakened immunity, who may have greater difficulty fighting infection. Pregnant women, who are generally considered a higher-risk group for complications from seasonal influenza. Risk also increases when someone has prolonged or close contact with an infected person, particularly in crowded or poorly ventilated environments. How Can You Stay Safe For most people, H1N1 does not require extensive medical intervention and recovery can occur with rest and appropriate supportive care. However, people at higher risk should seek medical advice early rather than waiting for symptoms to become severe. ICMR and NCDC guidance emphasises recognising warning signs and seeking timely medical care. Practical precautions include: Wash your hands regularly with soap and water or use an alcohol-based hand sanitiser. Cover your mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing. Avoid close contact with others when unwell, particularly vulnerable people. Stay home and rest while experiencing flu-like symptoms where possible. Avoid touching your eyes, nose and mouth with unwashed hands. Consider influenza vaccination after consulting a doctor, particularly if you belong to a higher-risk group. ICMR says the currently circulating strains are well matched with recommended Northern Hemisphere vaccine strains. Do not self-medicate with antibiotics, as they do not treat influenza viruses. Treatment decisions, including whether antiviral medicines are appropriate, should be made by a medical professional. People should seek prompt medical attention if they develop breathlessness, chest pain, low oxygen levels, confusion, severe weakness, dehydration or a persistent or worsening fever. NCDC guidance also identifies symptoms such as altered mental status, seizures, reduced urine output and breathing difficulty as warning signs requiring medical attention. Preparedness Matters Even Without A New Strain The government’s response reflects the distinction between a seasonal rise and the emergence of a new public-health threat. Nadda’s review focused not simply on case numbers but also on testing capacity, laboratory surveillance, hospital beds, critical-care facilities, oxygen-supported beds, ventilators, medicines and other essential supplies. The Union Health Ministry has said it is coordinating with states, hospitals and laboratories to strengthen surveillance, early detection and timely clinical management. Delhi’s health authorities have also sought to reassure residents about preparedness, saying hospitals have adequate capacity and that there is no shortage of beds, doctors, medicines or essential medical equipment. The broader lesson is that “no new strain” does not mean “no risk”. A familiar seasonal virus can still cause serious illness in vulnerable people, while a rise in cases can put additional pressure on healthcare systems. The Logical Indian’s Perspective The H1N1 situation shows why public-health communication must strike a careful balance between reassurance and responsibility. Rising numbers can understandably cause anxiety, but describing every surge as evidence of a dangerous new virus can create unnecessary fear; dismissing the increase altogether could leave vulnerable people without timely care. ICMR’s clarification provides reassurance, while continued surveillance and hospital preparedness ensure that reassurance is backed by action. In an age when health information can spread faster than the virus itself, how can we encourage a culture where evidence-based information, empathy and sensible caution replace both panic and complacency? The updated trivalent formulation targets two influenza A subtypes — A/H1N1 and A/H3N2 — and one influenza B/Victoria lineage virus, based on year-round surveillance data from the Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System (GISRS) spanning more than 100 countries. Photo: Designed by Freepik by freepik, https://creativecommons.org/public-domain/pdm/ A sick woman Strain changes driven by antigenic drift Influenza viruses undergo continuous antigenic drift — gradual mutations in surface proteins hemagglutinin and neuraminidase that allow the virus to evade existing population immunity. When the antigenic distance between circulating viruses and vaccine strains exceeds a threshold, vaccine effectiveness drops sharply. WHO's February 2024 composition meeting concluded that all three components from the 2023–2024 vaccine no longer matched the dominant circulating strains. The A/H3N2 component, historically associated with more severe seasons and higher hospitalization rates in older adults, has been updated to a clade 2.3.4.4b virus (A/Thailand/8/2022-like) replacing the previous A/Darwin/9/2021-like strain. Clinicians note this subtype often drives earlier epidemic onset. The A/H1N1 component shifts to an A/Victoria/4897/2022-like virus (clade 5a.2a.1), while the B/Victoria component moves to a B/Austria/1359417/2021-like virus (clade V1A.3a.2). The B/Yamagata lineage, absent from global circulation since March 2020, remains excluded from trivalent formulations. Sequential waves and population risk Epidemiological patterns show influenza A typically dominates early season activity (September–January), while B/Victoria circulation increases toward spring (February–April). This sequential pattern creates compound risk for vulnerable groups — children, adults over 65, and persons with chronic respiratory or cardiovascular conditions — who may face a second wave after physiological reserves are depleted by an initial infection. "When different virus types circulate simultaneously, the risk of severe disease increases substantially," said therapist Anna Kuznetsova in an interview with Pravda.Ru. "It is like trying to extinguish two fires at opposite ends of a house — the body's resources are finite." General practitioner Elena Morozova added that the spring B-wave is frequently underestimated: "People relax, thinking winter is over, yet the virus finds new opportunities for spread." Clinical presentation and diagnosis All three strains present with the classic influenza syndrome: abrupt onset of fever (often above 38.5°C), myalgia, headache, and nonproductive cough. Clinical differentiation from other respiratory viruses or between influenza subtypes is unreliable without laboratory confirmation. PCR-based multiplex assays remain the diagnostic standard for specific subtype identification, though antiviral treatment decisions in high-risk patients are often made empirically based on clinical syndrome and local epidemiology. Vaccination timing and limitations Health authorities recommend vaccination from late August through October, allowing approximately two to three weeks for protective antibody development before community transmission accelerates in September with school and workplace reentry. A second activity peak typically follows the winter holiday period when contact rates surge again. Vaccine effectiveness varies annually (typically 40–60% against laboratory-confirmed infection when well-matched) and is lower against H3N2 due to its faster antigenic evolution and egg-adaptation changes during manufacturing. Vaccination does not guarantee prevention of infection but consistently reduces risk of hospitalization, intensive care admission, and death, particularly in older adults and those with comorbidities. The experimental formulation is designed to address one of the central weaknesses of seasonal flu vaccination: conventional vaccines focus largely on hemagglutinin, a highly variable surface protein that can change sufficiently from year to year to reduce the match between a vaccine and circulating viruses. By presenting the more conserved M2 protein in a virus-like structure, the researchers aim to stimulate immunity that could remain effective against a wider range of influenza A viruses, including strains that current vaccines do not anticipate. The findings are scheduled for presentation on Aug. 24 at the American Chemical Society’s fall 2026 meeting. They remain preclinical, and the results in mice do not establish that the vaccine will protect people or provide long-lasting immunity. Even so, the approach combines two goals that have long challenged influenza researchers: identifying a viral target that changes slowly enough to support broad protection, and developing a manufacturing system that can produce vaccine material rapidly when a new strain begins to spread. The project is led by Fei Wen, a professor of chemical engineering at the University of Michigan, with doctoral student Trang Hoang as first author. Seasonal influenza vaccines are updated because the virus continually evolves, particularly in hemagglutinin, or HA. This protein forms the majority of the virus’s external surface and is readily recognized by antibodies generated after infection or vaccination. Mutations in HA can alter the sites, known as epitopes, that antibodies bind, allowing new variants to partially escape pre-existing immunity. Global health authorities monitor influenza circulation and recommend vaccine compositions months before each flu season, giving manufacturers time to produce doses. The process can work well when forecasts are accurate, but protection may be reduced when an emerging strain differs substantially from the selected vaccine viruses. The Michigan team took a different approach by focusing on M2, a small influenza protein involved in the virus’s life cycle. M2 functions as an ion channel in the viral envelope, helping regulate acidity inside virus particles as they enter host cells. Because its structure and activity are constrained by the need to support viral replication, M2 generally tolerates fewer mutations than HA. The researchers specifically use the portion of M2 exposed on the exterior of the virus, often called the M2 ectodomain, as an antigen. This region is relatively conserved across influenza A viruses, although it is present in much smaller quantities than HA and therefore does not normally dominate the immune response to an inactivated flu virus. That limited natural visibility is one reason M2 has attracted interest as a universal-vaccine target. An immune response directed toward conserved M2 regions may recognize viruses from several influenza A subtypes, rather than responding narrowly to the HA and neuraminidase proteins of one seasonal strain. Such immunity would not necessarily prevent infection in the same way as highly strain-matched HA antibodies. Instead, antibodies and other immune mechanisms targeting M2 could interfere with viral spread or help immune cells identify infected cells more efficiently, potentially reducing disease severity and transmission. The exact balance of these protective mechanisms will need to be established in further animal studies and, eventually, human trials. To make M2 more immunologically visible, the researchers assembled it on virus-like particles, or VLPs. These particles imitate the approximate size and shape of a virus but contain no influenza genome, so they cannot replicate or cause influenza infection. Their repetitive, ordered surfaces can help cross-link receptors on immune cells and promote antigen uptake, making VLPs useful platforms for vaccine development. In this case, the particles are covered with M2 protein rather than displaying the full collection of proteins found on an infectious influenza virion. The design therefore concentrates the immune system’s attention on a target that is normally overshadowed by the much more abundant HA. The manufacturing method begins with ordinary baker’s yeast that has been genetically modified to produce large quantities of M2. The yeast is grown in a nutrient-rich liquid, allowing the engineered cells to synthesize the viral protein. Researchers then use mild chemical treatment to remove the rigid cell wall while preserving the cell membrane and the molecular machinery associated with particle formation. According to the team, the wall-less yeast cells bud off M2-bearing particles that can be collected and purified. This strategy uses yeast as a biological production platform rather than relying on influenza virus grown in eggs or cell culture, and it could make it easier to scale production without handling infectious virus. Speed is a major potential advantage of the platform. Traditional egg-based influenza manufacturing can require roughly six months because candidate viruses must be selected, adapted to grow efficiently in eggs, propagated, harvested, purified and formulated. Production timelines can be shorter with cell-based or recombinant systems, but each has its own technical and regulatory requirements. The Michigan researchers say their yeast-based process can generate a substantial amount of vaccine material in about a month. If validated at industrial scale, that turnaround could be valuable during an outbreak, when health authorities may need to respond to a newly recognized strain rather than wait for the next routine seasonal update. In mouse experiments, the M2-based VLP vaccine generated strong immune responses and protected animals challenged with three different influenza strains, the researchers report. The breadth of the protection is important because it suggests that the formulation can produce functional immunity beyond a single closely matched virus. However, animal challenge studies are an early stage of vaccine evaluation. The team’s next step is to determine how long protection lasts in vaccinated mice and to characterize the antibodies and cellular responses responsible for it. Researchers will also need to test dosing, safety, repeat vaccination, protection against additional influenza subtypes and performance in animal models that more closely predict human responses. The technology has been licensed to Esperovax, which is exploring development of an oral vaccine based on the platform. An oral formulation could simplify administration and potentially improve access, although delivering vaccine antigens through the digestive system presents its own challenges. Before the vaccine can be tested in people, the researchers must demonstrate consistent manufacturing, define the composition and purity of the particles, and complete the toxicology and regulatory studies required for clinical development. A broadly protective flu vaccine remains a long-term objective rather than an immediate clinical option, but the yeast-derived M2 particles offer a strategy that links conserved viral biology with rapid, potentially flexible production. Young children and elderly people with underlying health conditions are among those considered more vulnerable to severe infection, according to the health department. India generally experiences two seasonal influenza peaks each year, between January and March and during the post-monsoon period. While H1N1 is the predominant influenza subtype in Delhi this year, H3N2 was the predominant subtype in the capital last year, the department said. The health authorities said surveillance guidelines remain in place throughout the year, with measures being taken to monitor, prevent and control the spread of influenza. Doctors are also stressing the importance of annual influenza vaccination, particularly for people at higher risk of developing complications. Commonly known as swine flu, H1N1 emerged in 2009 and was initially associated with influenza viruses found in pigs, which led to its popular name. The virus subsequently established sustained transmission among humans and now circulates as seasonal influenza A(H1N1)pdm09. According to Delhi Health Department data, the national capital had reported 1,777 H1N1 cases as of August 20, including 114 new cases in a single day. Delhi had recorded 2,602 influenza cases overall, of which 2,392 were Influenza-A and 210 were Influenza-B. The increase prompted the Delhi government to issue a health advisory and step up surveillance, while Union Health Minister JP Nadda reviewed the situation and the preparedness of hospitals. Dr Rajeev Chowdry, Director of Internal Medicine at Yatharth Hospital, Faridabad, said modern seasonal flu vaccines are designed to protect against the influenza viruses that surveillance indicates are most likely to circulate during the upcoming season. The H1N1 component is included alongside H3N2 and influenza B components in current trivalent influenza vaccines. H1N1 is a subtype of influenza A. According to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses currently circulating among humans are descendants of the virus that emerged in 2009. Like other influenza viruses, they have continued to undergo genetic and antigenic changes. This continuous evolution is one of the main reasons influenza vaccination is recommended every year. The virus circulating during one season may not be antigenically identical to strains that circulated in previous years. The World Health Organization therefore conducts global influenza surveillance and recommends vaccine compositions twice a year, separately for the northern and southern hemispheres, to ensure the best possible match with circulating strains. For the 2026-27 northern hemisphere influenza season, the WHO recommendation includes an H1N1pdm09-like strain in both egg-based and cell-culture or recombinant vaccines. The flu vaccine works by exposing the immune system to influenza antigens, allowing the body to develop antibodies without causing influenza infection from the vaccine itself. Following vaccination, the body needs time to develop protection, with the CDC stating that it generally takes around two weeks for protective antibodies to develop. Getting vaccinated before influenza activity becomes widespread is therefore preferable. Dr Chowdry said vaccination can reduce the risk of developing influenza and can also reduce the likelihood of severe disease if infection occurs. However, vaccination does not guarantee that a person will never contract influenza. Vaccine effectiveness varies from season to season depending on factors such as the match between vaccine strains and circulating viruses, the person's age and immune response and the particular influenza strain involved. “But vaccination can still reduce the risk of severe outcomes,” Dr Chowdry said. H1N1 symptoms are broadly similar to those caused by other seasonal influenza infections. People may develop fever, sore throat, cough, body aches, headache, chills and fatigue. In some cases, influenza can progress to serious complications such as pneumonia and respiratory failure. WHO India describes influenza as a contagious respiratory illness that can range from mild to severe. Severe infection can result in hospitalisation or death, with young children, pregnant women, older adults and people with certain underlying health conditions facing a higher risk of complications. The WHO estimates that seasonal influenza causes around one billion cases globally every year, including three to five million cases of severe illness and between 290,000 and 650,000 respiratory deaths annually. H1N1 spreads in much the same way as other seasonal influenza viruses. An infected person can release respiratory particles while coughing, sneezing or talking, which may then be inhaled by people nearby. Close contact with an infected person and contaminated hands or surfaces can also contribute to transmission. Dr Chowdry said the virus is highly contagious and can survive in the environment for a period of time. He also stressed that H1N1 spreads from person to person and is not acquired by eating properly cooked pork products. Annual vaccination is recommended because immunity can decline over time and influenza viruses continue to evolve. The WHO considers health workers, older adults, pregnant women and people with certain chronic medical conditions among the priority groups for seasonal influenza vaccination. People with conditions affecting the lungs, heart, kidneys, liver, nervous system or metabolism may face a greater risk of complications. Those with weakened immune systems are also more vulnerable, while children and older adults remain important groups because severe influenza can disproportionately affect them. Health authorities generally recommend getting vaccinated before influenza activity rises in a particular area, while allowing around two weeks for the immune response to develop. CDC guidance says September and October are generally suitable months for vaccination in the northern hemisphere, although vaccination can continue later while influenza viruses are circulating. Dr Chowdry advised people, especially those at higher risk of complications, to discuss the appropriate timing and vaccine formulation with their doctor. Along with vaccination, maintaining basic respiratory hygiene can help reduce transmission. Regular handwashing with soap and water or an alcohol-based hand sanitiser, along with avoiding close contact with people who are coughing or showing flu-like symptoms, can reduce the risk of infection. People who develop significant flu symptoms, particularly those at higher risk of complications, should not automatically assume they have a routine cold. Early medical assessment can be important in severe, progressive or high-risk cases, as antiviral medicines may be useful when influenza infection is suspected or confirmed and treatment is medically indicated. records.content: Kerala Karnataka records 4,212 influenza cases; Health Dept says H1N1 rise is seasonal With Karnataka reporting 4,212 influenza cases so far this year, the Health Department has stepped up surveillance and preparedness measures while saying the current H1N1 rise is within the state’s normal seasonal pattern. Karnataka has recorded 4,212 laboratory-confirmed influenza cases across 32 districts so far this year, with the Health Department attributing the current rise in H1N1 cases to the state’s usual seasonal pattern and urging people not to panic. According to surveillance data from the Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP), 4,212 influenza cases had been confirmed in the state as of August 22, 2026. H1N1 is a strain of the influenza A virus that can cause seasonal flu. Common symptoms include fever, cough, sore throat, body ache and fatigue. Bengaluru accounts for the majority of the cases. The Greater Bengaluru Authority (MSU) area has reported 2,070 cases so far this year, compared to 2,587 in 2025 and 1,189 in 2024. Bengaluru Urban has recorded 1,011 cases, broadly comparable to 961 cases in 2025 and 991 in 2024. The Health Department said influenza generally records two seasonal peaks in Karnataka — between January and March and again between July and September. The current increase in cases therefore falls within the state's usual seasonal pattern. Health Minister UT Khader chaired a review meeting with senior health officials from the state and districts to assess preparedness to manage the seasonal rise in influenza. The department said government health facilities have adequate infrastructure, essential medicines and other supplies to handle a possible increase in cases. Surveillance for Influenza-Like Illness (ILI) and Severe Acute Respiratory Infection (SARI) has also been strengthened in line with guidelines issued by the World Health Organization and the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. Surveillance is being carried out through designated sentinel sites under the ICMR-NCDC network for pan-respiratory virus surveillance, as well as through the Viral Research and Diagnostic Laboratories (VRDL) network. The department said laboratories have sufficient consumables to ensure timely sample collection and testing. Health facilities have been directed to maintain adequate stocks of essential supplies, including personal protective equipment, N95 masks and Oseltamivir, an antiviral medication used to treat influenza. Healthcare workers have also been sensitised to identify ILI and SARI cases early, assess risk and provide appropriate treatment. Private hospitals and healthcare facilities have been asked to follow state protocols for screening, testing and treatment of H1N1 cases. They have also been directed to report confirmed cases to surveillance authorities through the IHIP platform. As part of efforts to prevent transmission, the department has reinforced respiratory and hand hygiene measures in healthcare facilities and stepped up public awareness campaigns through print, electronic and social media. The Health Department has advised people to cover their nose and mouth while coughing or sneezing, wash their hands regularly with soap and water, drink plenty of fluids and isolate themselves if they develop flu-like symptoms. records.content: Kerala Karnataka records 4,212 influenza cases; Health Dept says H1N1 rise is seasonal With Karnataka reporting 4,212 influenza cases so far this year, the Health Department has stepped up surveillance and preparedness measures while saying the current H1N1 rise is within the state’s normal seasonal pattern. Karnataka has recorded 4,212 laboratory-confirmed influenza cases across 32 districts so far this year, with the Health Department attributing the current rise in H1N1 cases to the state’s usual seasonal pattern and urging people not to panic. According to surveillance data from the Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP), 4,212 influenza cases had been confirmed in the state as of August 22, 2026. H1N1 is a strain of the influenza A virus that can cause seasonal flu. Common symptoms include fever, cough, sore throat, body ache and fatigue. Bengaluru accounts for the majority of the cases. The Greater Bengaluru Authority (MSU) area has reported 2,070 cases so far this year, compared to 2,587 in 2025 and 1,189 in 2024. Bengaluru Urban has recorded 1,011 cases, broadly comparable to 961 cases in 2025 and 991 in 2024. The Health Department said influenza generally records two seasonal peaks in Karnataka — between January and March and again between July and September. The current increase in cases therefore falls within the state's usual seasonal pattern. Health Minister UT Khader chaired a review meeting with senior health officials from the state and districts to assess preparedness to manage the seasonal rise in influenza. The department said government health facilities have adequate infrastructure, essential medicines and other supplies to handle a possible increase in cases. Surveillance for Influenza-Like Illness (ILI) and Severe Acute Respiratory Infection (SARI) has also been strengthened in line with guidelines issued by the World Health Organization and the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. Surveillance is being carried out through designated sentinel sites under the ICMR-NCDC network for pan-respiratory virus surveillance, as well as through the Viral Research and Diagnostic Laboratories (VRDL) network. The department said laboratories have sufficient consumables to ensure timely sample collection and testing. Health facilities have been directed to maintain adequate stocks of essential supplies, including personal protective equipment, N95 masks and Oseltamivir, an antiviral medication used to treat influenza. Healthcare workers have also been sensitised to identify ILI and SARI cases early, assess risk and provide appropriate treatment. Private hospitals and healthcare facilities have been asked to follow state protocols for screening, testing and treatment of H1N1 cases. They have also been directed to report confirmed cases to surveillance authorities through the IHIP platform. As part of efforts to prevent transmission, the department has reinforced respiratory and hand hygiene measures in healthcare facilities and stepped up public awareness campaigns through print, electronic and social media. The Health Department has advised people to cover their nose and mouth while coughing or sneezing, wash their hands regularly with soap and water, drink plenty of fluids and isolate themselves if they develop flu-like symptoms. People have also been advised to avoid touching their eyes, nose and mouth, refrain from self-medication, and avoid crowded places, unnecessary gatherings and shaking hands while symptomatic. The department has also advised against reusing napkins. People experiencing symptoms have been advised to seek care at the nearest government health facility. The Health Department said there was no need for panic over the rise in cases, but urged people to follow recommended precautions and seek timely medical attention to help limit the spread of seasonal influenza. IMAGE: Union Health Minister JP Nadda chairs a review meeting on the H1N1 influenza preparedness, in New Delhi, August 21, 2026Photograph: @MoHFW_INDIA X/ANI Photo Key Points H1N1 influenza cases are increasing in Delhi and North India, consistent with seasonal flu activity. Experts confirm the H1N1 strain is not new or more virulent, alleviating panic. High-risk groups, including the elderly, young children, pregnant women, and those with chronic illnesses, should take extra precautions. Symptoms often include fever, cough, and body ache; severe warning signs like breathlessness require immediate medical attention. Most H1N1 infections are mild and self-limiting, resolving within three to five days with rest and hydration. H1N1 influenza cases have increased in Delhi and parts of North India in recent weeks, with experts advising people, particularly those at higher risk of complications, to take precautions but stressed that there is no evidence of the virus becoming more virulent. Understanding The H1N1 Strain Speaking to PTI Videos, former WHO chief scientist and former ICMR director general Dr Soumya Swaminathan said H1N1 is a known strain of influenza and not a new virus. "There is no evidence of a major antigenic shift or that the virus has become more virulent or dangerous," Dr Swaminathan said, adding that the recent increase in cases was consistent with seasonal influenza activity, particularly during the monsoon and winter months. The strain that caused the 2009 swine flu pandemic has continued to circulate globally. Swaminathan said that most people recover from the infection with adequate rest, fluids and symptomatic treatment. Who Is At Risk And What Are The Symptoms? However, elderly people, children, particularly those below five years of age, pregnant women and those with underlying chronic illnesses are at greater risk of complications. Warning signs such as breathlessness, bluish lips or nails, inability to eat or drink, altered consciousness, rapid breathing, vomiting or unusual irritability in children warrant prompt medical attention, Swaminathan said. Former AIIMS director Dr Randeep Guleria said H1N1 cases were currently rising in Delhi but were expected to decline as the monsoon recedes. He advised people, especially those in high-risk groups, to take precautions against influenza infection. Physician, public health and health policy expert Dr Chandrakant Lahariya said H1N1 was not a new influenza subtype. People with diabetes, hypertension or obesity, along with pregnant women, elderly persons and children, may be at higher risk of complications, he said. Those experiencing flu-like symptoms such as fever, cough, headache and body ache should consult a doctor and avoid taking antibiotics unless prescribed, Lahariya said. Patients should get adequate rest, stay hydrated, maintain electrolyte balance and ensure sufficient food intake during the illness, he added. Recognising Severe Complications Severe influenza can lead to complications such as pneumonia, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and, in some cases, brain infection, said Dr Rashmi Kapoor, head of the Department of Paediatrics at Regency Healthcare, Kanpur. Parents should ensure that children remain adequately hydrated and seek immediate medical attention if they develop breathing difficulties or seizures, Kapoor said. She also advised parents to consider seasonal flu vaccination for children. Expert Advice And Public Reassurance Dr Abhishek Tandon, consultant in respiratory and sleep medicine at Medanta, Lucknow, said H1N1 influenza was widespread in north India but there was no need to panic. Most cases present as a mild and self-limiting upper respiratory infection, with symptoms including fever, sneezing, runny nose, sore throat, dry cough, breathlessness, weakness and fatigue, he said. Tandon advised against taking antibiotics or steroids over the counter and said high-risk patients and those with underlying health conditions may require antiviral treatment, such as oseltamivir, following medical consultation. Most infections resolve within three to five days, Tandon said. On Sunday, ICMR sources said that no new strain of H1N1 has been identified and there is no cause for panic. The Influenza strains currently circulating are "well matched with the vaccine strains recommended for the Northern Hemisphere", they said. "The rise in H1N1 cases has brought preventive vaccination back into the conversation," said Dr Bharat Gopal, senior director, Respiratory and Sleep Medicine, Medanta Mediclinic, Defence Colony and Medanta-The Medicity. records.content: The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) on Sunday (August 23, 2026) said that the Influenza A (H1N1) viruses currently circulating in the country belong to the A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1) pdm09-like virus strain. It clarified that no new strain of H1N1 has been identified and there is no cause for panic. “These viruses belong to clade 6B.1A.5a2a, subclade D.3.1.1, and have been in circulation since 2025. The Influenza strains currently circulating are also well matched with the vaccine strains recommended for the Northern Hemisphere,” ICMR said. “Seasonal influenza, including H1N1, is mostly self-limiting,” it added. Common symptoms of the illness include fever, cough, headache, and body ache, and most people recover with appropriate care and rest. However, young children, elderly persons, and individuals with underlying medical conditions may be at a greater risk of complications. If symptoms persist, worsen, or become severe, consultation with a doctor is advised, it said. The Union Health Ministry has said that it is closely monitoring the situation through regular surveillance and is undertaking necessary public health measures. India has registered a rise in seasonal Influenza A(H1N1) cases, commonly called swine flu, this monsoon, especially in major cities. Delhi has reported 1,777 confirmed H1N1 cases so far this year, including 114 new cases on August 20. Karnataka has registered over 4,000 cases, with more than half reported from Bengaluru. Rising influenza activity has also been reported in Mumbai, Chennai and parts of Kerala. National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC) data show that H1N1 activity was relatively low in 2021 (778 cases, 12 deaths) after the pandemic period, but rebounded sharply in 2022 (13,202 cases, 410 deaths) and remained substantial in 2023 (8,125 cases, 129 deaths). By June 2024, India had already recorded 7,215 cases and 150 deaths, and year-end numbers were higher. NCDC’s 2025 reporting shows that H1N1 continued to circulate across multiple States. NCDC maintains a nationwide influenza surveillance network and publishes State-wise data and H1N1 treatment/prevention guidelines. It recommends seasonal influenza vaccination based on WHO strain recommendations. For the 2025–26 season, India’s recommended trivalent vaccine included H1N1, H3N2 and B/Victoria components, with circulating Indian H1N1 strains aligning with vaccine strains. “People at higher risk should consider annual vaccination and seek medical advice promptly if flu symptoms become severe,” Anil Bansal of the Delhi Medical Association said. India World Sport Data Health Opinion Science Entertainment Premium Videos Podcast Photos Visual Stories Specials TH Explains eBooks TH Games Newsletter Lit For Life The Huddle Home Sci-Tech Health No new H1N1 strain in India, existing vaccines sufficient, says ICMR Influenza strains currently circulating are well matched with the vaccine strains, and the seasonal flu is self-limiting, ICMR said, adding that people with underlying medical conditions are at risk of complication Updated - August 23, 2026 10:06 pm IST - New Delhi Bindu Shajan Perappadan READ LATER SEE ALL Remove Image used for representational purposes only. | Photo Credit: Getty Images/iStockphoto The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) on Sunday (August 23, 2026) said that the Influenza A (H1N1) viruses currently circulating in the country belong to the A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1) pdm09-like virus strain. It clarified that no new strain of H1N1 has been identified and there is no cause for panic. H1N1 cases on the rise, experts say no cause for alarm “These viruses belong to clade 6B.1A.5a2a, subclade D.3.1.1, and have been in circulation since 2025. The Influenza strains currently circulating are also well matched with the vaccine strains recommended for the Northern Hemisphere,” ICMR said. “Seasonal influenza, including H1N1, is mostly self-limiting,” it added. Common symptoms of the illness include fever, cough, headache, and body ache, and most people recover with appropriate care and rest. However, young children, elderly persons, and individuals with underlying medical conditions may be at a greater risk of complications. If symptoms persist, worsen, or become severe, consultation with a doctor is advised, it said. H1N1 surge: hospital footfall increases as doctors flag risks The Union Health Ministry has said that it is closely monitoring the situation through regular surveillance and is undertaking necessary public health measures. India has registered a rise in seasonal Influenza A(H1N1) cases, commonly called swine flu, this monsoon, especially in major cities. Delhi has reported 1,777 confirmed H1N1 cases so far this year, including 114 new cases on August 20. Karnataka has registered over 4,000 cases, with more than half reported from Bengaluru. Rising influenza activity has also been reported in Mumbai, Chennai and parts of Kerala. National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC) data show that H1N1 activity was relatively low in 2021 (778 cases, 12 deaths) after the pandemic period, but rebounded sharply in 2022 (13,202 cases, 410 deaths) and remained substantial in 2023 (8,125 cases, 129 deaths). By June 2024, India had already recorded 7,215 cases and 150 deaths, and year-end numbers were higher. NCDC’s 2025 reporting shows that H1N1 continued to circulate across multiple States. NCDC maintains a nationwide influenza surveillance network and publishes State-wise data and H1N1 treatment/prevention guidelines. It recommends seasonal influenza vaccination based on WHO strain recommendations. For the 2025–26 season, India’s recommended trivalent vaccine included H1N1, H3N2 and B/Victoria components, with circulating Indian H1N1 strains aligning with vaccine strains. “People at higher risk should consider annual vaccination and seek medical advice promptly if flu symptoms become severe,” Anil Bansal of the Delhi Medical Association said. H1N1, commonly known as swine flu, is a type A influenza virus that causes respiratory infections. Here's all you need to know about the H1N1 flu vaccine: Who can take it? When can it be administered? Why do you need it? Why is the H1N1 vaccine important? Director General of Health Services (DGHS) Dr Loveneesh G Krishna told news agency ANI last week that vaccination can help decrease the severity of H1N1 infection. Vaccination is a “preventive measure”, and not a cure altogether. It helps your body build immunity, so you are less likely to get sick with the H1N1 virus in the first place. “H1N1 is a seasonal influenza that spreads very easily from one person to another. Therefore, we need to take some preventive measures, which include wearing a mask to cover your nose and mouth, washing your hands frequently with soap and water, keeping indoors well-ventilated, and taking vaccines to decrease the severity,” Krishna was quoted as saying. “The flu vaccine is the best protection against the flu. If you get the flu vaccine, you are 60% less likely to need treatment for the flu,” Max Healthcare explained on its website. Vaccination is not a recommended intervention for swine flu-infected patients. Which influenza vaccine to take? Who can take them? The ICMR said in a statement on Sunday that circulating H1N1 strains match the recommended Northern Hemisphere vaccine strains. The National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC) has also recommended the use of the “NH [Northern Hemisphere]” vaccine in the 2026-2027 influenza season. 1. The Indian Medical Association (IMA) had said in 2015 that Influenza vaccines can prevent flu caused by human strains, which is "recommended for children above 6 months; Adults > 50 years of age; Patients with pulmonary, cardiovascular, renal, hepatic, neurologic, hematologic disorders and diabetes mellitus; pregnant females and Health care providers." "The inactivated vaccine can be given to the above groups. The Live attenuated influenza vaccine (intranasal spray) can be given only to persons aged 2-49 years (not to pregnant females)," the IMA added. NOTE: It's better to consult a doctor before getting an influenza vaccine. Speak with a healthcare provider first if you have specific allergies, comorbidities, a history of severe reactions, or an acute moderate-to-severe illness with a fever. When to take the vaccine? It takes about two weeks after vaccination for antibodies to develop and provide protection against influenza virus infection. In the meantime, you are still at risk of getting the flu. That's why it's better to get vaccinated early in the fall, before the flu season really gets underway. What if you are already sick with the H1N1 flu? If you have a fever, you should wait until it is gone before getting a flu shot, Max Healthcare stated. It explained that one can get a flu shot if they have a respiratory illness without a fever or another mild illness. According to the sources, the influenza strains currently circulating in the country are well matched with the vaccine strains recommended for the Northern Hemisphere. AI Summary AI-generated summary, reviewed by editors Indian health authorities confirm no new H1N1 strain circulates despite rising cases in Delhi and India; current viruses match vaccine strains, surveillance continues, and medical consultation is advised for severe symptoms. Seasonal influenza, including H1N1, is generally self-limiting. Common symptoms include fever, cough, headache and body ache, with most patients recovering with adequate care and rest. However, young children, elderly people and those with underlying health conditions face a higher risk of complications. The Influenza A (H1N1) pdm09 viruses currently circulating in India belong to the A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1) pdm09-like strain, the ICMR sources said. The viruses fall under clade 6B.1A.5a2a and subclade D.3.1.1 and have been circulating since 2025. People experiencing persistent, worsening or severe symptoms have been advised to consult a doctor promptly. Authorities are continuing to monitor the situation through regular surveillance and are taking necessary public health measures. Delhi has recorded more than 2,300 Influenza-A cases so far this year, including over 1,777 H1N1 cases as of Friday. The health department reported 114 H1N1 cases on Thursday alone. The Delhi government has issued a health advisory urging residents to maintain respiratory hygiene, avoid crowded places and seek medical attention when necessary. He called for continued vigilance, robust surveillance and proactive preparedness. Delhi Health Minister Pankaj Kumar Singh also attended the meeting. Nadda reviewed national surveillance and epidemiological trends, including influenza-like illness (ILI) and severe acute respiratory infection (SARI), along with testing, laboratory surveillance and the preparedness of healthcare facilities to manage seasonal influenza cases. He stressed the importance of closely monitoring influenza trends and ensuring the timely detection and management of any unusual increase or clustering of cases. The preparedness of healthcare facilities in Delhi was also assessed, including the availability of hospital beds, critical care facilities, oxygen-supported beds, ventilators, essential medicines, diagnostic services and other key supplies. [Wikimedia Commons] Share Tweet Share Share Email Comments India is experiencing an increased number of H1N1 swine flu cases but the country is not facing the threat of a new strain of the virus, scientists from the Indian Council of Medical Research said. The currently available influenza vaccines also continue to be effective against circulating strains of the virus, The Hindu reported. Viruses such as the Influenza A (H1N1) pdm09 are in circulation in the country that are similar to the A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1) pdm09-like strain, which has been prevalent in the country since 2025, ICMR reported. These viruses have also shown a strong match against vaccine strains that have been recommended for use in the northern hemisphere. “There is no need to panic,” officials with the ICMR have said. “Seasonal influenza, such as H1N1, is typically a mild condition that is self-limiting” ICMR officials said other common symptoms include cough, headache and body aches. Most people recover within a few days with proper care, adequate rest and treatment. This year, more than 1,777 cases have been observed in the country’s capital, Delhi alone and that is with the broader jump in influenza cases, information coming out of the Health Department indicates. higher than the corresponding annual figure for 2024.According to data released by the state health department on Monday, Greater Bengaluru recorded 2,070 influenza-positive cases till August 22, compared with 2,587 cases during all of 2025 and 1,189 in 2024. The figures indicate a substantial rise even before the current monsoon influenza season has run its course.Bengaluru Urban has also reported 1,011 cases so far this year, against 961 in 2025 and 991 in 2024. Bengaluru Rural and Bengaluru South have recorded 26 cases each till August 22.Across Karnataka, 4,212 laboratory-confirmed influenza cases have been reported in 2026 so far, compared with 4,583 cases in the whole of 2025 and 3,903 in 2024. IANS Created On: 24 Aug 2026 11:22 AM ISTComment Share : X Delhi's Safdarjung Hospital fully equipped to manage H1N1 cases, seasonal illnesses A− Font size A+ Select Hans India Now FOLLOW ON Google News New Delhi: Safdarjung Hospital in Delhi has said it is fully equipped to manage patients suffering from swine flu, or H1N1 influenza, as well as other seasonal illnesses, with necessary medicines, treatment facilities and supportive care available. In a statement, the hospital said patients presenting with influenza-like symptoms are being appropriately assessed and fast-tracked for timely medical attention. Treatment is being provided according to the clinical requirements of individual patients and prevailing medical guidelines. “The hospital is fully equipped to manage cases of swine flu and other seasonal illnesses, with necessary medicines, treatment facilities and supportive care available,” the hospital said. “Patients presenting with influenza-like symptoms are appropriately assessed and fast-tracked for timely medical attention. Appropriate treatment is provided as per clinical requirements and prevailing guidelines,” it added. The hospital further said it continues to monitor such cases and has adequate arrangements in place for their management. The statement comes amid increased attention on H1N1 and seasonal influenza cases in Delhi. Health authorities and hospitals have been closely monitoring patients reporting influenza-like symptoms, particularly those requiring timely medical intervention because of breathing difficulties or other complications. Safdarjung Hospital said its existing arrangements are adequate to manage such patients and provide supportive care wherever required. The hospital’s emphasis remains on early assessment, timely treatment and continued monitoring of influenza-like illnesses. H1N1 is a subtype of influenza A virus that causes respiratory infection. It became widely known as “swine flu” during the 2009 influenza pandemic. The virus subsequently became part of the seasonal influenza viruses that circulate among humans. Common symptoms of influenza can include fever, cough, sore throat, headache, body aches, fatigue and a runny or blocked nose. In many cases, people recover within several days to about a week. However, influenza can sometimes lead to serious complications, particularly among older adults, young children, pregnant women and people with certain underlying health conditions. Severe respiratory symptoms, persistent high fever, breathing difficulty, chest discomfort, confusion or a worsening condition may require prompt medical evaluation. Influenza spreads mainly through respiratory droplets and particles released when an infected person coughs, sneezes or talks. Maintaining good hand hygiene, covering coughs and sneezes and avoiding close contact with people who are unwell can help reduce transmission. Seasonal influenza vaccination is also an important preventive measure, particularly for people at higher risk of complications. ICMR sources said the influenza strains currently circulating in the country are “well matched with the vaccine strains recommended for the Northern Hemisphere”. The circulating Influenza A (H1N1) pdm09 viruses belong to the A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1) pdm09-like strain. They are part of clade 6B.1A.5a2a, subclade D.3.1.1, and have been circulating since 2025. Union Health Minister J P Nadda reviewed the H1N1 situation and preparedness across the country on Friday, with particular attention to Delhi. Delhi Health Minister Pankaj Kumar Singh also attended the meeting. Nadda reviewed national surveillance and epidemiological trends, influenza-like illness (ILI) and severe acute respiratory infection (SARI) patterns, testing and laboratory surveillance. He also assessed healthcare preparedness, including hospital beds, critical care and oxygen-supported beds, ventilators, essential medicines, diagnostics and other supplies. The ICMR sources said the situation is being monitored through regular surveillance. They advised people to consult a doctor if symptoms persist, worsen or become severe. The surveyor collected responses of nearly 32,000 respondents. Written By Fareha Naaz Updated24 Aug 2026, 10:16 AM IST H1N1 Cases near 1,800 in Delhi: Why Is the Health Minister Holding a Meeting Today? Explained AI Quick Read A survey conducted across Delhi NCR recently revealed that residents of around 54% households have members infected with flu, showing viral fever like symptoms at a time when H1N1 cases are on the rise. The findings of this Local Circles report published on 23 August are based on 32,000 responses collected from across Delhi, Gurugram, Noida, Faridabad and Ghaziabad. Around 69% respondents were men and 31% were women. The survey further revealed that 23% households surveyed have four or more individuals currently down with flu fever like symptoms. Around 16% of the respondents were reported to have two to three symptomatic members while 15% households surveyed had at least one individual down with viral like fever. This suggests sustained transmission inside homes, implying that 39% of households surveyed had two or more members symptomatic at the same time. Also Read | No new H1N1 strain in circulation, vaccines remain effective: ICMR The national capital registered 159 fresh influenza cases on 20 August, out of which 114 were H1N1, commonly known as swine flu, cases. With seasonal influenza in focus due to surge in cases, Delhi reported 2,392 influenza-A cases this year. This year, Delhi's cumulative swine flu tally has reached 1,777 with H1N1 being the predominant strain. At the same while H1 cases tally stood at 37, H3 at 138 and other influenza cases at 440. Also Read | H1N1 cases in Delhi higher, ‘severe’: Experts warn, advisory issued | 10 points It should be noted that the official case count includes only citizens who visited a hospital or laboratory to be tested. There is a shortfall in reported figures as many others who contracted the disease but recovered at home remain unaccounted. ICMR issues statement on H1N1 virus In the wake of rising swine flu cases, the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) issued a statement on Sunday, clarifying that no new strain of influenza A (H1N1) has been identified in the country. ICMR scientists emphasized that there is no cause for panic regarding the seasonal influenza virus currently circulating. Also Read | Delhi records 1,777 H1N1 cases; Centre lists symptoms as flu rises A senior ICMR scientist said, “The influenza A (H1N1) pdm09 viruses currently circulating in India are similar to the A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1) pdm09-like virus strain. These viruses belong to clade 6B.1A.5a2a and subclade D.3.1.1 and have been in circulation since 2025,” ANI reported. With many Delhi-NCR residents suffering from fever, cough, sore throat, headache, body aches, chills and fatigue, ICMR called the seasonal influenza "mostly self-limiting". According to the Council, most people recover with appropriate care and adequate rest, although young children, elderly people and individuals with underlying medical conditions remain most at risk.
